title: Crowdfunding, Public Insurance, and the Economics of Sentiment: An Empirical and Narrative Analysis of Medical Fundraising in India
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Crowdfunding, Public Insurance, and the Economics of Sentiment: An Empirical and Narrative Analysis of Medical Fundraising in India

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only secondary, fully anonymized data derived from publicly accessible medical crowdfunding campaigns. No interaction with campaign organizers, donors, or patients occurred, and no identifiable personal information was collected, analysed, or reported. All variables used, including campaign location at the state level, dates, fundraising amounts, donor counts, campaign tags, and sentiment classifications, were aggregated and anonymised prior to analysis. The research was conducted solely for academic purposes and poses no risk to individuals or groups. The project complies with ethical guidelines governing privacy, confidentiality, and non-disclosure.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether medical crowdfunding in India acts as a substitute for or complement to public health insurance, using a seven-year dataset of over 5500 campaigns. Cross-state regressions show no evidence that higher PM-JAY insurance disbursements reduce crowdfunding intensity; instead, states receiving greater public funds often produce more negative campaign narratives, indicating substantial residual costs. Spatial analysis reveals that hospital-bed density aligns more closely with crowdfunding reliance than insurance financing, while GDP per capita is linked to modestly more positive sentiment. To explain why some campaigns succeed, the paper draws on behavioural economics, narrative theory, emotional contagion, and the identifiable-victim effect, showing that donors respond more readily to compelling moral stories than to statistical need. Crowdfunding therefore reflects gaps in infrastructure, digital access, and institutional protection rather than pure market substitution. The conclusion outlines policy reforms to integrate crowdfunding data into health planning and to strengthen protections in an increasingly sentiment-driven landscape.

title: How Innovations Increase the Value of Human Time
affiliations: Market Platform Dynamics

detail.title: How Innovations Increase the Value of Human Time
detail.abstract: Entrepreneurs, businesses, and policymakers should treat human time as a measurable, improvable resource with immense potential for value creation. This paper examines time as humanity's most valuable and constrained asset. A rough estimate of value of the national time stock, in the U.S., puts it at around $4.5 quadrillion, dwarfing traditional assets such as housing ($55 trillion) and fixed capital ($87 trillion). The paper identifies nine partly overlapping levers through which disruptive innovations enhance time's value: saving time through new goods and services; making time by extending longevity; enriching time by expanding experiences; monetizing time through increased productivity; enjoying time via leisure activities; trading time through attention markets; investing time in education; accelerating time through faster information transmission; and multiplying time through more people with more time. Historical examples demonstrate how innovations from electrification to digital platforms have transformed human time. GDP fails to account for most time-related value creation. The paper proposes a "time scorecard", based on the nine levers as key performance indicators and existing economic methods for valuing time tradeoffs, to complement GDP. The time scorecard could provide governments, and others, guidance for policies and investments that maximize the value of human time.

title: From Innovation to Default: Impact of Patent Activity on Credit Risk
affiliations: University of Zurich, University of Zurich and University of Zurich - Department Finance

detail.title: From Innovation to Default: Impact of Patent Activity on Credit Risk
detail.abstract: We investigate how firm-level innovation-measured via patent grants, citations, and high-quality inventions-affects corporate credit risk and CDS pricing. Using a panel of 191 firms, we first calibrate an inverse-Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck intensity model to each firm's CDS term structure and extract risk-neutral survival probability curves. We further orthogonalize the patentbased features and estimate Arellano-Bond regressions on the factors that characterize the survival probability curves, demonstrating that innovation alters the level, slope, and curvature of the curves. We then embed patent-based covariates directly into the intensity specification and analyze how they affect the CDS prices within a no-arbitrage model: the augmented model reduces in-sample and out-of-sample pricing errors by up to 15% relative to a leverage-and-volatility baseline. Finally, we compute model spread deltas with respect to innovation covariates to quantify the economic impact on CDS spreads, finding that higher innovation activity systematically tightens spreads-especially at longer tenors. Overall, our findings show that patent-driven covariates provide incremental information on credit risk beyond traditional metrics and offer practical enhancements for intensity-based CDS pricing.

title: Protecting Migrant Children and the Best Interests of the Child: Lessons from the European Case

detail.title: Protecting Migrant Children and the Best Interests of the Child: Lessons from the European Case
detail.abstract: This article examines how the principle of the Best Interests of the Child (BIC) is applied in the context of migrant children, focusing in particular on unaccompanied foreign minors in the European Union. On paper, the EU has a dense, multi-layered system of child protection, rooted in the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the case law of supranational courts. In practice, however, the full realisation of the BIC is held back by a familiar combination of factors: a structural tension between security-oriented migration policies and rights protection, the wide discretion enjoyed by Member States, and an adult-centred understanding of "protection" that often turns the child's right to be heard into a purely formal step. The article argues that there are two main levels of difficulty. First, general migration rules and practices frequently collide with protective principles. Second, even measures explicitly designed for children tend to reproduce rigid categories of vulnerability and a narrow, monocultural model of the family. At the same time, bottom-up practices-civic networks, NGOs, guardians, mediators-operate as forms of "de facto" subsidiarity and sometimes manage to secure more meaningful protection and participation. Yet these actors are themselves constrained by administrative logics and performance indicators, which may turn solidarity into a regulated and depoliticised form of humanitarianism. Drawing on the sociology of childhood, the article proposes to treat the BIC as a dynamic and relational principle that recognises children as social actors, with their own cultures and forms of agency. A brief comparison with Brazil and Africa suggests that without an adequate epistemological and value framework, even the most advanced legal systems tend to produce weak and fragmented protection. The article concludes by outlining some theoretical and practical directions for a more equitable and culturally sensitive protection of migrant children that takes the BIC seriously.

title: Ever Closer Union: Ever Present But Often Overlooked
affiliations: University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Ever Closer Union: Ever Present But Often Overlooked

publicationDetails.detailsText: Edinburgh School of Law Research Paper No. 2025/29
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Edinburgh School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The phrase "ever closer union" has been present in what are now the EU Treaties since 1957. This article presents a diagnosis of its role within the framework of those Treaties, highlighting key changes in relation to both the context and content of European integration, which could potentially affect the meaning ascribed to "ever closer union". In fact, it is a phrase without fixed meaning, which is often overlooked by those making or interpreting law and policy or involved in presenting proposals. Scholars have sometimes sought to elevate "ever closer union" in order to give it a "higher" and potentially constitutional significance within the framework of the European integration, but in practice the phrase retains more of a symbolic than a practical significance, with limited obligations on the part of Member States actively to pursue any given aspect of the putative "ever closer union".

title: Performance and Risk Analysis of ESG versus Non-ESG Robo-Advisory Portfolios: Evidence from the German Market
affiliations: and University of Duisburg-Essen

detail.title: Performance and Risk Analysis of ESG versus Non-ESG Robo-Advisory Portfolios: Evidence from the German Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as no human participants or sensitive personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This study examines ESG vs. Non-ESG Portfolios of four German robo-advisors from December 2019 to June 2024. We evaluate 24 portfolios across three risk tiers and six benchmarks using performance and risk metrics. Using traditional (mean, standard deviation), higher (skewness, kurtosis) and risk-adjusted indicators (Sharpe ratio, Jensen's alpha, value at risk, conditional value at risk), we analyse whether and to what extent ESG portfolios offer advantages over conventional strategies. Our results show that, on average, ESG portfolios exhibit slightly lower volatility and a more robust tail risk profile. During periods of pronounced market volatility (for example, the COVID-19 downturn), sustainable portfolios frequently exhibit smaller peak-to-trough losses compared to conventional strategies. Our provider-level analysis shows that the effectiveness of ESG integration hinges on precise asset selection, as well as the frequency and timing of portfolio rebalancing. Drawing on proprietary performance data and established econometric techniques, this study advances understanding of how sustainability considerations interact with risk management and return generation in algorithmically managed portfolios.

title: Macroeconomic Announcements and the Repricing of Earnings Risk
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and UBC - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Macroeconomic Announcements and the Repricing of Earnings Risk
detail.abstract: Macroeconomic announcements lead to the repricing of earlier firm-specific earnings news, generating heterogeneity in risk compensation in the cross section of equity returns. When firms announce earnings, investors form joint beliefs about both firm-specific and aggregate components. Subsequent macro announcements reveal information about the aggregate state of the economy, prompting investors to reassess the firm-specific component of the prior earnings news. We develop a dynamic general equilibrium model in which investors rationally learn from both earnings and macro announcements to quantify the importance of this repricing channel. Empirical evidence supports the model’s predictions: firms with recent earnings systematically underperform those without on macro-announcement days, with the effect strongest for firms whose earnings-day returns comove most with the market.

title: Cognitive Resilience in Military and Law Enforcement Personnel: Neuropsychological Insights and Implications for High-Stress Performance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cognitive Resilience in Military and Law Enforcement Personnel: Neuropsychological Insights and Implications for High-Stress Performance
detail.abstract: Cognitive resilience-the ability to maintain or regain cognitive functioning during and after stress-is a critical factor in the performance and well-being of military and law enforcement personnel. This article explores the neuropsychological foundations of cognitive resilience, its predictors, and its role in sustaining operational performance under conditions of acute and chronic stress. Drawing on recent research, including Pelz (2024), this study examines how factors such as executive functioning, emotional regulation, and psychological hardiness contribute to resilience in high-stress roles. It also reviews training protocols and selection practices that can enhance these capacities. While resilience has traditionally been viewed as a psychological construct, this article emphasizes its cognitive and neurobiological dimensions, arguing that targeted interventions at the cognitive level can improve readiness and recovery in demanding professions. Recommendations are provided for integrating cognitive resilience assessments into recruitment, training, and post-deployment support systems for personnel in both military and law enforcement contexts.

title: The Use of State Discipline to Sanction Attorneys General and Other High-Ranking Legal Officers
affiliations: University of Connecticut School of Law

detail.title: The Use of State Discipline to Sanction Attorneys General and Other High-Ranking Legal Officers
detail.abstract: The United States Attorney General, state attorneys general, and high-ranking officials in their offices, like all lawyers, are subject to rules of professional conduct. Increasingly, when they push the boundaries of these rules and other well-established professional norms, individuals and organizations are filing state lawyer disciplinary grievances against them. While some see troubling conduct by these high-ranking government officials, others view these disciplinary grievances as politically motivated. State lawyer disciplinary authorities often try to avoid addressing these grievances. This article examines why it is nonetheless important for state lawyer disciplinary authorities-which are agencies of state courts-to act on certain grievances. It explains why the political process cannot be relied upon to respond to serious misconduct by these high-ranking legal officers, and why other institutions that could address misconduct are ill-equipped or unlikely to act. The article then describes developments in one state that make it more difficult for some grievants to file actionable grievances and for state disciplinary authorities to pursue certain grievances against these high-ranking officials. It explains why these developments are misguided. It then suggests some ways to accommodate the concerns and competing interests at stake when state disciplinary authorities receive grievances against these officials. The article also identifies some types of professional misconduct by these officials that are sufficiently problematic that state disciplinary authorities should act to address those grievances.

title: Gendered Perceptions of Safety and Comfort in a Heritage Tourist Corridor: The Case of Pangeran Mangkubumi Street, Yogyakarta

detail.title: Gendered Perceptions of Safety and Comfort in a Heritage Tourist Corridor: The Case of Pangeran Mangkubumi Street, Yogyakarta

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human subjects research requiring institutional review board approval. Data were collected through an anonymous online questionnaire distributed voluntarily via social media. All participants provided electronic informed consent prior to completing the survey. No personal or identifiable information was recorded. The research complied with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and UNESCO’s guidelines for social science research ethics. detail.abstract: This note examines gender-based perceptions of safety and comfort in Yogyakarta’s Pangeran Mangkubumi pedestrian corridor, part of the city’s philosophical axis linking the Tugu Monument with the Yogyakarta Palace. Using a descriptive quantitative approach, data were collected through an anonymous online survey of individuals who had walked along this corridor. Results show that 63.93% of respondents considered the path “quite safe” and 63.64% “quite comfortable.” Female respondents emphasized personal safety, while male respondents prioritized spatial efficiency and convenience. These gendered perceptions reflect broader urban health implications—safer and more comfortable sidewalks encourage physical activity, reduce anxiety, and enhance social well-being. The study provides practical insights for local governments and planners to improve pedestrian environments through inclusive, gender-sensitive design.

title: Wealth Meets Value: The Role of Advice for High Net Worth Individuals
affiliations: University of Witten/Herdecke, , University of Esslingen and University of Witten/Herdecke

detail.title: Wealth Meets Value: The Role of Advice for High Net Worth Individuals
detail.abstract: Financial advice has often been criticised for failing to generate value in retail settings, where conflicts of interest and product-driven incentives prevail. Using a proprietary dataset of nearly 1,000 private banking portfolios observed over 40 months, we examine whether advice creates measurable value in the wealth management context and mitigates behavioural biases related to overconfidence, the disposition effect, and home bias. Our results reveal that advice significantly reduces portfolio volatility and the home bias, while it enhances diversification. Effectiveness diminishes among highly active and financially literate investors, indicating limits to behavioural correction. Overall, financial advice in the HNWI segment distinguishes itself by fee-based incentives and enduring client relationships that align advisor and client interests.

title: Literature Review on New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Literature Review on New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC)
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the theoretical and empirical evolution of the Phillips Curve through the lens of modern New Keynesian macroeconomics. While the traditional unemployment–inflation relationship has long been viewed as unstable, recent advances attribute its variability to the interaction of expectations, nominal rigidities, and structural features such as openness and imported marginal costs. The review synthesizes key developments in the New Keynesian Phillips Curve, including forward-looking price setting, hybrid indexation, sticky-information dynamics, and small open-economy extensions. Empirical evidence across advanced, emerging, and transition economies reveals substantial heterogeneity in slope, persistence, and the relative weight of backward- and forward-looking components, particularly across tranquil and recessionary periods. The findings highlight that the Phillips Curve is conditional rather than structural, with inflation dynamics fundamentally shaped by the credibility of monetary policy, the structure of expectations, and the sensitivity of marginal costs to domestic and external shocks.

title: Singular Value Decomposition as Optimal Unsupervised Ridge Regression
affiliations: AbleMarkets.com

detail.title: Singular Value Decomposition as Optimal Unsupervised Ridge Regression
detail.abstract: We establish a fundamental connection between ridge regression and singular value decomposition (SVD) as solutions to related penalized optimization problems. Ridge regression minimizes ∥y-Xβ∥ 2 + λ∥β∥ 2 for fixed penalty λ > 0, requiring cross-validation for optimal penalty selection. We prove that SVD eigenvectors v i solving (X ′ X-λ i I)v i = 0 satisfy an analogous optimality condition where penalties λ i (eigenvalues of X ′ X) are determined optimally from the data's covariance structure. This characterization shows that SVD is an unsupervised regularization method that automatically selects direction-specific penalties maximizing explained variance. Empirical validation demonstrates SVD's superior signal detection (68%-100% accuracy) compared to ridge regression (0%-27%) and LASSO (0%-23%) across multiple noise distributions. The method provides both theoretical optimality and computational efficiency for high-dimensional feature selection problems.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks Meet Asset Pricing
affiliations: University of Bremen

detail.title: Recurrent Neural Networks Meet Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: This paper proposes the conditional recurrent neural network (C-RNN), a flexible and interpretable recurrent factor model for capturing the dynamic structure of asset returns. The C-RNN conditions latent factors and factor loadings on observable variables and allows both to follow vector autoregressive dynamics. Using U.S. stock data, the C-RNN outperforms existing models in return prediction, and a simple zero-investment strategy achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.30 versus 0.82 for instrumented principal component analysis-the state-of-the-art benchmark model. These results highlight the value of combining temporal dependencies with conditioning information and show that few factors but many characteristics are needed to model returns.

title: Rethinking Education in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Skills, Exams, and Labor Market Alignment
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Rethinking Education in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Skills, Exams, and Labor Market Alignment

declarations.ethicsApproval: This is not an empirical paper. Ethical approval does not apply

detail.abstract: Traditional memory-heavy examination systems are increasingly misaligned with the skills required in the AI era. Drawing on literature from assessment studies, labor economics, and the emerging debate on AI and education, we show that exams focused on rote memorisation and short-term information recall crowd out deeper learning and fail to predict performance in complex, relationally intensive jobs. Using Italy as a paradigmatic case-with its reliance on oral university exams and highly selective, memorisation-based professional competitions for judges and diplomats-we document a structural mismatch between what is tested and what the labour market demands. We propose a three-factor model of individual productivity in the AI era, where output depends on: (i) spiritual capital-a bundle of relational, emotional and ethical capacities; (ii) competenciesformal education and learning-by-doing, including digital skills; and (iii) the effective use of AI and digital tools. Current exam systems observe only a narrow slice of this space, largely ignoring spiritual capital and AI-complementary skills. We then derive policy implications for curriculum and assessment reform, arguing for a shift from memory overload towards tasks that resemble real professional activities and explicitly cultivate spiritual capital. Finally, we outline concrete design principles for "second-generation" university and professional exams that preserve the advantages of competitive, anonymous selection (speed, impartiality, signalling of effort) while better aligning education with the needs of an AI-rich economy. The resulting architecture has, in our perspective, the potential to increase graduation rates, reduce mismatch, and improve labour-market outcomes.

title: Smaller Banks, Smarter Lending? Evidence from the Commercial Real Estate Market
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business, Cornell University and Cornell SC Johnson College of Business

detail.title: Smaller Banks, Smarter Lending? Evidence from the Commercial Real Estate Market
detail.abstract: We study the role of community banks in commercial real estate (CRE) lending during the Covid-19 pandemic, a period of heightened uncertainty in a market characterized by informational frictions. Using bank-level Call Reports, property-level loan data from MSCI, and leasing outcomes from Compstak, we compare lending decisions and associated outcomes of community and large banks during this period. We show that community banks increased CRE lending during the pandemic, primarily within their local markets, and in large part by financing properties previously funded by large banks. Community banks also experienced lower foreclosure rates on loans issued during this period and stronger operating performance of the properties financed. These findings are consistent with a model of banking competition in which community banks can leverage superior local information against the lower cost of capital of large banks when uncertainty is high.

title: Healthy Minds, Brighter Futures: Sociological Methods to Explore and Improve Public School Mental Health Systems for Marginalized K-12 Youth in the U.S.
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Healthy Minds, Brighter Futures: Sociological Methods to Explore and Improve Public School Mental Health Systems for Marginalized K-12 Youth in the U.S.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: According to the National Center for Education Statistics, over half of K-12 public schools nationwide are unable to offer effective mental health services to their students. These statistics further reveal that socioeconomically underserved students are more likely to face this problem than the general student population. This paper proceeds by using three sociology-based methods to address this topic. First, structural issues that contribute to this nationwide problem are explored. These issues include poverty among youth, lack of funding for mental health services in public schools, and geographic constraints. This paper’s second sociological method explores the effectiveness of universal mental health screening in schools to help support students in need. The final method demonstrates the importance of inclusive interventions to help these students. Overall, these three sociology-based approaches offer ways to both understand and remedy this problem.

title: Are Socially Responsible Funds Viable?
affiliations: London School of Economics (LSE), London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Finance, Department of Finance and HEC Paris - Finance Department

detail.title: Are Socially Responsible Funds Viable?
detail.abstract: We study the viability of socially responsible (SR) funds when investors are small, have social preferences, and can cheaply invest in other ways. In a static setting, SR "impact" funds, which engage with dirty firms at a cost, cannot exist due to free riding, regardless of the type of social preferences. SR exclusion funds with reduced ownership of dirty firms can exist, but only if investors' social preferences are "warm glow," i.e., tied to the extent of ownership. In a dynamic setting, we demonstrate a symbiosis between SR fund types-the existence of exclusion funds allows impact funds to profit by buying and then cleaning up dirty firms.

title: Railway Carrier’s refusal to draw up a Commercial Act: Civil Liability and Recent Russian Case Law

detail.title: Railway Carrier’s refusal to draw up a Commercial Act: Civil Liability and Recent Russian Case Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human participants or experimental research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: The article analyses the legal consequences of a railway carrier's refusal to draw up a commercial act as required by Article 119 of the Russian Railway Transport Statute. Recent case law from 2023-2025 demonstrates that courts hold carriers liable for damages even without the act, treating such refusal as bad-faith conduct under Article 10 of the Civil Code. The study shows that claimants may rely on alternative evidencegeneral form reports, regulatory inspection files, correspondence-and may file antitrust complaints to obtain administrative orders against the carrier. The paper's novelty lies in systematizing judicial practice and proposing criteria under which the absence of a commercial act does not bar damage recovery. Practical recommendations are offered for carriers and shippers to adapt internal procedures and mitigate legal risks.

title: Keep it Simple: Central Bank Communication and Asset Prices *
affiliations: Queen Mary, University of London, Vanguard Asset Management Ltd and ETH Zürich

detail.title: Keep it Simple: Central Bank Communication and Asset Prices *
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of different types of Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) communication and its complexity on financial markets from 1999-2023. We classify communication into simple versus complex using a Readability Index. We find complex communication is associated with greater and prolonged asset price volatility. We also extend the UK high-frequency monetary policy shock measures to include speeches. We find speeches have enduring effects on asset prices. Combining both findings, we show that accounting for simple communication and including speeches produces a more powerful instrument for estimating the macroeconomic effects of monetary policy shocks.

title: Client Due Diligence and Risk Allocation in the Conclusion and Performance of a Freight Forwarding Agreement

detail.title: Client Due Diligence and Risk Allocation in the Conclusion and Performance of a Freight Forwarding Agreement
detail.abstract: The article examines contractual risk allocation in freight forwarding where cargo delivery is contingent on the shipper’s release and the forwarder lacks a mandate to deliver without such release. Using a focused case from the Moscow Arbitrazh Circuit, it shows that when the contract allocates the risk of the shipper’s conduct to the client, storage and container-use charges stem from the agreed disposition model rather than the forwarder’s conduct, provided the forwarder documented notices and escalation. The methodology combines doctrinal analysis of civil and maritime rules with a case-based mapping of contractual clauses to the legal control over release. The contribution is an operational client due-diligence checklist: a workable release mechanism, an agreed “delivery-against-security” option, a time-stamped communications protocol, SLA windows and expense caps aligned with transport documents. This configuration reduces dispute risk and breaks legal causation with the forwarder’s conduct in the absence of a contractual mandate to deliver without release.

title: Risk-Seeking Motives and Speculative Investment
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, Brown University, Harvard University, Harvard University and Sogang University

detail.title: Risk-Seeking Motives and Speculative Investment
detail.abstract: Why do some individuals make high-risk financial investments? Using millions of linked records from Korea's leading credit bureau, telecom provider, and credit card company, we study the determinants and consequences of speculative activity. We classify explanations for high-risk financial behaviors into two types: those that overcome risk aversion, either through optimistic beliefs or desire for entertainment, and those driven by risk-seeking preferences, endogenously generated from desperation or aspirational motives (à la Friedman and Savage, 1948). Consistent with true risk-seeking motives, crypto app usage is higher among individuals with more unsecured debt, higher spending, and fewer assets, and rises after unemployment and new borrowing. Crypto app usage is also disproportionately concentrated among young and early-middle-aged men. Crypto speculation carries consequences: among crypto users, bitcoin price drops lead to lower consumption and increased delinquency, while a price boom is followed by increases in homeownership. Survey data show that crypto holders are more risk-seeking in choice tasks and more optimistic in their beliefs about crypto returns. In a stylized model, we show that when households are both risk-seeking and overoptimistic, risk-seeking preferences can amplify the negative effects of overoptimism.

title: Virtual Reality and Real Virtuality: The Economy of Perception in the Age of the Metaverse

detail.title: Virtual Reality and Real Virtuality: The Economy of Perception in the Age of the Metaverse
detail.abstract: In the twenty-first century, the boundary between the real and the virtual has become increasingly indistinct, reshaping the foundations of economic value. This study explores how Virtual Reality (VR) and Real Virtuality (RV) converge within the metaverse to form a hybrid “meta-economy” in which perception, attention, and symbolic participation function as key resources. A bibliometric analysis of 1,505 Scopus-indexed publications (2018–2024) reveals four dominant research clusters—marketing, technological innovation, AI applications, and blockchain-based virtual economies—highlighting the field’s interdisciplinarity. By integrating insights from economic theory, media studies, and digital capitalism, the paper theorises the shift from material to perceptual value as the defining logic of the post-real economy.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of country-specific geopolitical risk on capital flow volatility and asset markets across 29 emerging and advanced economies over the period 2000–2023. Using panel regressions and a panel structural vector autoregression framework, the results show that geopolitical risk raises bond yields and leads to exchange rate depreciation, with stronger and more persistent effects in emerging economies. Asset markets for advanced economies are affected mainly through lower equity prices. The impact on capital flow volatility is slightly higher on average for advanced economies but remains more persistent for emerging economies. Greater financial development, higher central bank independence, and lower public debt mitigate the adverse effects of geopolitical risk on both capital flows and asset markets. These findings highlight the importance of strong macroeconomic fundamentals and institutional frameworks in building resilience against geopolitical shocks.

detail.abstract:
This lecture explores the evolving architecture of international sanctions and their influence on cross-border commercial activity, with a particular focus on contractual performance and risk allocation. Sanctions have become one of the most powerful instruments of foreign policy, employed to compel changes in behavior through economic and legal pressure rather than military force.

The presentation begins by outlining the normative basis for sanctions under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which empowers the Security Council to impose measures in response to threats to international peace and security. It further contrasts multilateral sanctions with unilateral regimes adopted by the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, emphasizing their extraterritorial enforcement and the legal nexus required to assert jurisdiction over foreign actors.

A substantial portion of the lecture addresses the contractual consequences of sanctions under different legal systems. It examines how sanctions may qualify as force majeure or hardship events under Article 79 of the CISG, English contract law, and Article 401 of the Russian Civil Code, and how parties can mitigate exposure through the inclusion of specialized sanctions and compliance clauses.

Finally, the presentation discusses practical compliance mechanisms, focusing on due diligence in international trade transactions, vessel screening, and red flags associated with shadow fleet operations. The objective is to equip legal practitioners, compliance officers, and business leaders with a structured understanding of how sanctions reshape the legal environment of international commerce and what measures can be adopted to ensure lawful and resilient contract performance.

title: Diplomatic Dialogues in the Shadow of War: How Interwar Failures Shaped United Nations Conflict Resolution Strategies
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Diplomatic Dialogues in the Shadow of War: How Interwar Failures Shaped United Nations Conflict Resolution Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper explores how international conflict resolution has developed over time, emphasizing the shift from the League of Nations to the United Nations. It posits how the League's interwar period diplomatic and institutional failures shaped the UN’s core structures and diplomatic strategies. The study looks into the failures of the League of Nations, particularly its response—or lack thereof—to the Manchurian and Abyssinian crises, to determine what lessons were used to design the UN. It also looks into these lessons and their impact on the framework of the UN, especially the creation of the Security Council with its enforcement capabilities. The paper conducts an analysis of early UN case studies, including the Korean War, the Suez Crisis, and the Congo Crisis, to assess the implementation and impact of the new framework on collective security and peacekeeping. Through these case studies, the research provides an analysis of the evolution of institutions of contemporary international relations. It reaches the understanding that although the UN was far from a flawless answer to the problems of the world, its establishment represented a profound and realistic step forward in the chronology of global relations because it,” learned from the mistakes of the previous body in order to construct a stronger framework for the preservation of world safety and order.

detail.abstract: Amid the looming insolvency of the U.S. Social Security system, this study examines Americans' awareness of potential benefit reductions and their anticipated behavioral responses. Survey results reveal that only one-fifth of respondents know about the projected 23% cut in future benefits, with Black and Hispanic individuals five percentage points less likely to be aware. When informed of potential reductions, most current and future beneficiaries indicated they would reduce spending, delay retirement, or claim benefits later. Limited awareness of impending cuts could lead to suboptimal financial decisions, underscoring the need for targeted public education initiatives.

title: From Monetary Revolution to Financial Vassalage: The Intellectual Origins, Practical Alienation, and Systemic Co-optation of Cryptocurrency

detail.title: From Monetary Revolution to Financial Vassalage: The Intellectual Origins, Practical Alienation, and Systemic Co-optation of Cryptocurrency
detail.abstract: This paper traces the strange and ironic journey of cryptocurrency, from its revolutionary origins to its current role as a handmaiden to the very system it sought to overthrow. Born from the ashes of the 2008 financial crisis, crypto was steeped in the Austrian School's disdain for central banking—a techno-utopian attempt to create a "money without a state." Yet, in less than two decades, this ambitious project has unfolded in a series of paradoxes. Bitcoin, designed as peer-to-peer electronic cash, failed utterly as a practical currency, its wild price volatility forcing it to retreat into the niche of "digital gold." The subsequent wave of DeFi (decentralized finance), aiming to rebuild the entire financial system from the ground up, instead morphed into a speculative casino, where leverage and structural inequities dwarfed ideals of openness. The most profound irony, however, lies in the rise of stablecoins. These dollar-pegged tokens, meant to solve crypto's instability, became a Trojan horse. They have effectively tethered the entire crypto ecosystem to the U.S. dollar, transforming a would-be rebel into a potent new distributor of dollar hegemony. We argue that this story is not one of simple failure, but of systemic co-optation. The crypto movement, for all its disruptive rhetoric, has been largely absorbed and repurposed by the existing financial order. Far from challenging the system, it has become an unwitting engine of its expansion into the digital realm. The recent, seemingly benign, embrace of crypto by regulators like the U.S. Federal Reserve is not an endorsement of its ideals, but the final act of this co-optation—a modern-day "recruitment of the rebel alliance." The history of crypto thus serves as a powerful lesson: technological innovation, when it ignores the stubborn realities of power and institutional inertia, is more likely to be harnessed by the status quo than to overthrow it.

title: One Fed, Many Voices: Coordinated Communication vs. Transparent Debate

detail.title: One Fed, Many Voices: Coordinated Communication vs. Transparent Debate

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2025-23
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We analyze 481 speeches by FOMC members since 2007, excluding official press conferences. Combining high-frequency financial data with text analysis, we identify monetary policy surprises and measure each speech’s similarity to the Chair’s press conference preceding it. On average, monetary surprises around these speeches have no significant effect on inflation expectations or stock prices. Yet, speeches closely aligned with the Chair’s press conference amplify policy transmission, while less coordinated remarks dilute earlier effects on yields, inflation expectations, and equities. A general equilibrium model with incomplete information rationalizes these findings.

title: Bank Credit Supply and the Unemployment Rate
affiliations: Mount Allison University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Bank Credit Supply and the Unemployment Rate
detail.abstract: There is a strong negative relationship between U.S. bank credit and the unemployment rate since the mid-1980s. In this paper, I ask: Is there a causal connection between changes in the supply of bank credit and the observed fluctuations of the unemployment rate? If so, what are the transmission mechanisms governing such a relationship? To answer these questions, I proceed down two paths. First, I use a bank credit supply measure estimated by Bassett, Chosak, Driscoll, and Zakrajšek (2014) to document the effect that bank credit supply shocks have on the unemployment rate in a VAR model. The results suggest that a one percent contraction in the supply of bank credit leads to a 0.3 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate. Moreover, bank credit supply shocks account for about 30% of the volatility in the unemployment rate. Second, I rationalize these results by incorporating a banking sector into an otherwise standard DSGE model with labor search frictions and nominal rigidities. Unlike standard banking models-which restrict banks to intermediaries of pre-accumulated loanable funds-this paper allows banks to finance loans through deposit (i.e., money) creation as described in McLeay, Radia, and Thomas (2014) and Bundesbank (2017). Matched firms must obtain a bank loan to purchase their inputs before production. When banks contract credit, there are fewer funds for firms to purchase their capital and labor inputs and the cost of borrowing rises. This lowers the firms' benefit of matching thereby lowering the benefits of posting a vacancy. As a result, fewer vacancies are posted and labor market tightness falls. In both empirical and model settings, a contraction in bank credit supply leads to a typical recession: GDP, investment, and labor market tightness fall while the cost of external finance and the unemployment rate rise.

title: Prenatal Program Participation and Child Reading Achievement: Evidence from the PSID Child Development Supplement (PSID Dataset)

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether prenatal participation in two U.S. safety-net programs—the Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) nutrition program and Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC)—is associated with children’s later reading achievement. Using nationally representative data from the PSID Child Development Supplement (analytic N=1,845), we estimate multiple regression models controlling for child age, family income, low birth weight, and home learning environment. We find that WIC and AFDC participants exhibit lower reading scores on average; however, these negative coefficients likely reflect underlying socioeconomic disadvantage rather than causal effects of the programs. Among covariates, home environment quality and family income are the strongest positive predictors of reading outcomes. The results highlight the centrality of postnatal home learning conditions in shaping cognitive development and suggest that prenatal support programs may be more effective when integrated with sustained early-learning interventions. This study contributes observational evidence on the long-term correlates of prenatal public assistance using a policy-relevant, nationally representative dataset.

title: Beyond Arrow's Impossibility: A Formal Proof that Negative Vote Satisfies all Five Fairness Criteria

detail.title: Beyond Arrow's Impossibility: A Formal Proof that Negative Vote Satisfies all Five Fairness Criteria
detail.abstract: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem demonstrates that no ranked voting system can simultaneously satisfy five desirable fairness criteria. This working paper proves that a binary directional choice mechanism-the Negative Vote-satisfies all five conditions. Under this system, voters may form complete ordinal rankings but then choose whether to cast a vote FOR their top-ranked candidate or AGAINST their bottom-ranked candidate. This two-stage process provides sufficient information to escape Arrow's constraints without requiring voters to quantify preference magnitudes. The proof demonstrates that Unrestricted Domain, Non-Dictatorship, Pareto Efficiency, Independence of Irrelevant Alternatives, and Collective Rationality are all satisfied.

title: The Boundary Principle: Why Transformation Follows the Same Four Stages in Minds, Machines, and Matter

detail.title: The Boundary Principle: Why Transformation Follows the Same Four Stages in Minds, Machines, and Matter
detail.abstract: Transformation is typically treated as a domain-specific process: psychologists analyze identity crises, AI researchers study catastrophic forgetting, and physicists investigate the breakdown of classical models. This paper argues that these events reflect a single architectural mechanism-the Boundary Principle. The Principle proposes that coherent systems, when pushed to the limits of their predictive frameworks, undergo a four-stage sequence of Expansion, Suspension, Confrontation, and Integration. This sequence is first illustrated through intuitive cases in psychology and machine learning and then demonstrated rigorously through mathematical and physical invariants: the Golden Ratio φ, the exponential base e, π, Planck's constant h, and the Feigenbaum constants δ and α. Each invariant becomes visible only through boundary-induced instability, indicating that transformation follows a universal structural pattern. The Boundary Principle generates falsifiable predictions across AI, neuroscience, immunology, and psychology, positioning it as a candidate for a general law governing how systems reveal deeper invariants at the edge of coherence.

keywords: Evidence Standards for Logs and Metrics

detail.abstract:
Modern automated systems evolve continuously through deployment pipelines, data-driven adjustments and learning models whose internal behaviour can shift in ways that escape occasional inspection. Traditional legal supervision, built around documents and ex-post reviews, struggles to track risks that emerge at this operational layer. This paper argues for a framework of oversight grounded in technical literacy, drawing on early regulatory experiences with algorithmic audits, AI impact assessments and risk-based supervision. The proposal emphasises practical capacities: traceable data governance, defensible evidence from logs and metrics, structured inspection routines and controlled testing environments. These elements support a form of reliability understood not as a guarantee but as a disciplined organisational habit. The paper suggests how legal institutions can incorporate such practices and how insights from Site Reliability Engineering can inform a more realistic standard of responsibility in automated environments.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the drivers of Rwanda's export growth over the period 2020-2025 using a bilateral partner × year panel. Using annual merchandise exports from UN Comtrade and partner-level macroeconomic variables from the World Bank WDI, I estimate partner fixedeffects models with year fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors to isolate time-varying determinants of Rwanda's export behavior. I also consider dynamic specifications (lagged exports) estimated via system GMM to account for persistence and endogeneity. The paper discusses implications for trade policy and regional integration, with specific attention to trade concentration (top partners such as UAE and DRC) and commodity composition (gold, coffee, tea, base metals). Data sources, reproducible R code, and pre-analysis plans are provided to maximize transparency and replicability.

detail.abstract:
This study investigates the existence and dynamics of property price bubbles in major Indonesian cities from 2010 to 2025 using a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) regression approach. The research aims to identify the macroeconomic and financial factors influencing rapid housing price growth, including interest rates, GDP per capita, credit expansion, and urban population growth.

The 2SLS model is employed to address endogeneity between property prices and credit variables, ensuring unbiased parameter estimation. Results indicate significant evidence of speculative bubbles during periods of low interest rates and high credit growth, particularly in Jakarta, Surabaya, and Medan.

The findings highlight the critical role of monetary policy and banking regulation in mitigating systemic risks within Indonesia’s real estate sector. This study contributes to the empirical understanding of asset price bubbles in emerging markets and provides policy recommendations for sustainable housing market development.

title: The Energy of the Anthropocene

detail.title: The Energy of the Anthropocene
detail.abstract: The planet is in trouble. Much of this is the result of how we produce and use energy. As Vaclav Smil has made very clear, neither our economy nor our civilization could exist without energy.[1] That said, we must take a careful look at our relationship with energy to ensure it does not harm our planetary home. It is the only one we have. Cherish it we must.

title: A Multi-Agent Market Simulation with Fundamental and Behavioural Dynamics
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Multi-Agent Market Simulation with Fundamental and Behavioural Dynamics
detail.abstract: Financial markets exhibit complex behaviours-fat-tailed return distributions, volatility clustering, and prolonged deviations from fundamental values-that traditional equilibrium models fail to explain fully. This study develops a multi-agent market simulation in which heterogeneous traders interact within a single synthetic equity market. Agents employ distinct strategies-trend-following, mean-reversion, and fundamental value investing-while the asset's intrinsic value evolves through a geometric Brownian motion process with optional company feedback. Prices emerge endogenously from a supply-demand clearing mechanism that aggregates individual orders. The model reproduces several key stylized facts of fundamental markets, including heavytailed log-return distributions (kurtosis 10.6), weak short-term autocorrelation, and persistent volatility clustering. Controlled experiments isolating agent types reveal that trendfollowers amplify volatility and tail risk, mean-reverting agents stabilize price dynamics, and fundamental traders anchor long-term equilibrium. Policy simulations show that microstructural interventions-such as order delays ("speed bumps") and incentives for more extended holding periods-can meaningfully reduce speculative volatility and tail events without eliminating market efficiency. Overall, the framework demonstrates how realistic market dynamics can arise from the interaction of simple behavioural heuristics. It provides a transparent, extensible platform for analyzing the systemic effects of trading behaviour and market regulation in a controlled, data-rich environment. This work was conducted as part of an independent research project under the mentorship of Anuj Awasthi , Vice President of Operations at CGIF, whose insights into market microstructure and behavioural trading dynamics provided valuable guidance during model development.

title: Sustainability-linked Loans and Financial Performance
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Sustainability-linked Loans and Financial Performance
detail.abstract: Using a sample of bank loans, I find that firms borrowing sustainability-linked loans (SLLs) experience credit rating upgrades and higher post-borrowing equity returns relative to firms borrowing conventional loans. Channel tests then indicate that these effects arise primarily through reduced financing costs channels. To rationalize the findings, I develop a model in which firms choose between SLLs and conventional loans: SLLs offer lower coupons conditional on meeting sustainability targets but incur additional borrowing and compliance costs. The model shows that the financing-cost reduction alone is sufficient to generate the observed credit improvements and equity outperformance.
